chapterTitle: Infrastructure and Application Monitoring with Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Grafana
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute live coding demo. Start by creating an AMP workspace. Then, launch an EC2 instance, SSH into it, and demonstrate installing and running the Node Exporter. screens.title: Infrastructure & Application Monitoring with AMP and AMG
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore how Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana let teams keep the Prometheus model they trust while removing operational overhead. You will learn why organizations favor Prometheus-format metrics for containerized workloads, how exporters expose metrics, the role a local Prometheus server plays when forwarding data using remote write, and how Managed Grafana visualizes those metrics with PromQL queries. We'll use concrete examples: Node Exporter producing host metrics, a Prometheus server configured for remote write to an AMP workspace, and a Grafana panel that computes C P U utilization. I'll point out common pitfalls such as incorrect IAM permissions or misconfigured Grafana data sources, and a simple check to validate metrics flow. By the end you'll understand the end-to-end flow from exporter to query, what parts you manage, and what AMP and AMG manage for you, so you can plan a migration or deploy a new monitoring stack with confidence.

Amp + Grafana: Managed Prometheus at Scale

Remote Write

Grafana

Local Prometheus → AMP
Scrape targets, then remote_write to AMP for storage and query.

screens.title: Why choose AMP over self-hosted Prometheus or CloudWatch
screens.narratorSegment: Start with the problem many teams face: self-hosted Prometheus is familiar and flexible but becomes difficult to operate at scale. You must manage storage, high availability, backups, and horizontal scaling when ingesting millions of samples. AMP addresses those operational concerns by offering a managed, Prometheus-compatible backend. That means you keep existing exporters, PromQL queries, and dashboards while shifting storage, scaling, and availability to the managed service. Contrast AMP with CloudWatch: CloudWatch is excellent for native AWS metrics and aggregated service telemetry, but it is not Prometheus-native. If your stack relies on Prometheus exporters or Kubernetes metrics, AMP preserves label semantics and PromQL semantics that CloudWatch may not. A common misconception is that AMP replaces all observability needs; instead, view AMP as a drop-in scalable backend for Prometheus data while CloudWatch remains useful for AWS-specific metrics. Example: when migrating a Kubernetes cluster, retaining Prometheus labels lets you reuse alerting rules and Grafana dashboards without rework. The takeaway is practical: choose AMP when you want Prometheus compatibility and to avoid running the storage layer yourself, and keep CloudWatch for service-level or platform events where it already excels.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: AMP preserves Prometheus semantics while removing storage and scaling overhead; CloudWatch complements AMP for AWS-native signals.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Choice: AMP vs Self-Managed
When to prefer AMP
If you rely on Prometheus exporters and PromQL, want built-in scaling, and prefer a managed storage and retention model, AMP is a strong fit. It lets you preserve existing queries, dashboards, and labels.
Operational burden removed
No need to manage long-term storage, scaling shards, or HA Prometheus clusters.
Prometheus compatibility
Keep PromQL, labels, and exporters unchanged.
Retention & scale
AMP stores large volumes and supports multi-month retention without operator pain.
Where self-hosted or CloudWatch still fits
Self-hosted Prometheus gives maximum control and is useful for tiny workloads or edge cases where you need custom storage. CloudWatch is ideal for AWS-specific metrics and logs and integrates with other AWS services directly.
Self-hosted: full control
You manage scaling, backups, and performance tuning.
CloudWatch: AWS native
Use for service-level telemetry, logs, and events where CloudWatch is already instrumented.
Key Takeaway

Use AMP to keep Prometheus workflows and remove operational scaling and storage concerns; combine with CloudWatch when you need AWS-native signals.

Common mistake
Assuming AMP replaces CloudWatch entirely. Instead, treat them as complementary: AMP for Prometheus-format time-series, CloudWatch for native AWS service metrics.

screens.title: What is Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)?
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed service that provides a Prometheus-compatible ingestion, storage, and query backend. In practice this means you can keep your existing exporters and PromQL queries but avoid running the distributed storage and scaling systems yourself. AMP accepts Prometheus remote write traffic, stores samples for months, and exposes an A P I that AMP-aware clients and Grafana can query. A concrete example: run a Prometheus server in your cluster that scrapes node_exporter and kube-state-metrics, and configure remote_write to forward those samples to your AMP workspace endpoint. AMP handles ingestion at scale, sharding, and retention so your operations team doesn't need to manage long-term storage. A common misconception is that AMP changes the Prometheus data model. It does not: AMP preserves metric names and labels, so existing alerts and dashboards continue to work. The practical takeaway is to treat AMP as a managed, drop-in backend that scales your Prometheus data and reduces operational toil. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › What is AMP?
AMP is a fully managed, Prometheus-compatible monitoring service. It accepts Prometheus remote write data, preserves the Prometheus data model, and provides long-term storage and availability without operator maintenance.
Scales
Handles large ingestion volumes and sharding concerns for you.
Prometheus-compatible
Keep labels, metrics, and PromQL semantics unchanged.
Retention
Stores time-series data for extended periods without local storage maintenance.
Concrete config example
# Example: Creating an AMP workspace via AWS CLI
aws amp create-workspace --alias my-devops-workspace
Use the workspace endpoint for Prometheus remote_write configuration on your Prometheus server.
Common misconception
AMP does not alter Prometheus metric semantics. Labels and metric names remain the same, so alerts and dashboards built for Prometheus continue to function.

screens.title: Prometheus Exporters — Role and common types
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus exporters are simple HTTP agents that expose application or host metrics in the Prometheus text format. The exporter model decouples metric collection from storage: exporters only expose metrics, and Prometheus scrapes them. Common exporters you will use include Node Exporter for host-level metrics like C P U, memory, and disk input and output; kube-state-metrics for Kubernetes object-level metrics such as pods and deployments; and application-specific exporters for software like Redis, MySQL, or Nginx. You can also instrument application code using Prometheus client libraries to expose custom application metrics. A concrete example: Node Exporter listens on port 9100 and exposes metrics at /metrics; Prometheus scrapes that endpoint at a configured interval. A frequent mistake is trying to push metrics directly from exporters to AMP; exporters are meant to be scraped by Prometheus. Instead, run a Prometheus server to scrape exporters and use Prometheus remote_write to forward metrics to AMP. Remember the practical rule: exporters expose, Prometheus scrapes, and AMP stores. This separation makes the pipeline modular and easier to debug. Prometheus Exporters — Role and common types means exporters expose metrics via http; prometheus scrapes them and then forwards samples to amp via remote_write.. In practical terms, how exporters expose metrics and which ones to use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Exporters expose metrics via HTTP; Prometheus scrapes them and then forwards samples to AMP via remote_write.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Prometheus Exporters
Exporters present metrics in Prometheus format on an HTTP endpoint. Prometheus scrapes these endpoints and gathers samples for each scrape interval. Exporters are not push clients; they are passive endpoints that expose current metrics.
Node Exporter
Exposes host-level metrics such as CPU, memory, and disk I/O, typically on port 9100.
kube-state-metrics
Exposes Kubernetes object metrics like pods, deployments, and replica counts.
App-specific exporters
Databases, caches, and web servers often provide exporters to expose internal metrics.
Example
Run Node Exporter on an EC2 instance and visit the /metrics path or curl it to verify it exposes numeric counters and gauges. Then configure Prometheus to scrape that endpoint regularly.
Common mistake
Expecting exporters to push to AMP directly. They should be scraped by Prometheus, which then remote_writes to AMP.
Pro tip
Use curl or a browser to check the exporter endpoint and sample metric names before configuring Prometheus scraping.

screens.title: Scrape to Remote Write: The data flow
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the data flow is critical for reliable monitoring. The typical pipeline starts with exporters exposing metrics on HTTP endpoints. A Prometheus server scrapes these endpoints at a configured interval, converting the textual metrics into time-stamped samples. Instead of storing those samples locally, a Prometheus server can be configured with remote_write to forward samples to an AMP workspace endpoint. Remote_write batches samples and sends them to AMP with optional queue and shard settings to control throughput. AMP then performs ingestion, indexing, and long-term storage. For visualization, AMG connects to AMP as a data source and uses PromQL to query the stored time-series. A concrete scenario: you deploy Node Exporter on each node, configure a cluster-local Prometheus to scrape node exporters and kube-state-metrics, and enable remote_write to AMP. Common mistakes include forgetting to adjust scrape intervals, not tuning queue_config when high cardinality metrics produce a lot of samples, or using exporters that expose too-frequent metrics that overwhelm the queue. The practical check is to validate each step: curl the exporter, verify Prometheus target status, and confirm samples appear in Grafana Explore.

keyIdea.text: Exporters → Prometheus scrape → Prometheus remote_write → AMP ingestion → AMG visualization with PromQL.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Scrape → Remote Write
Pipeline steps
  1. Exporter exposes metrics at /metrics.
  2. Prometheus scrapes endpoints at scrape_interval.
  3. Prometheus forwards samples via remote_write to AMP.
  4. AMP ingests and stores samples; AMG queries them with PromQL.
Validation checklist
  • curl exporter /metrics to confirm exposure.
  • Check Prometheus target page to ensure successful scrapes.
  • Watch Grafana Explore to validate samples appear from AMP.
Operational note
When high-cardinality metrics or high scrape frequency produce heavy sample volumes, adjust Prometheus queue_config and shard settings in remote_write to avoid dropped samples.
Common mistake

Assuming exporters push metrics; they must be scraped. Configure Prometheus to scrape then remote_write to AMP.

Key Takeaway
Verify each hop in the pipeline: exporter, scraper, remote write, and visualization to find where samples are lost.

keyIdea.title: Remote write essentials
keyIdea.text: Configure remote_write with your AMP workspace URL, sigv4 region, and tune queue_config to match scrape load.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Prometheus remote_write
Below is a literal example derived from the chapter. Replace placeholders for your environment before use. Pay attention to the sigv4 block and queue_config values when your scrape load is high.
# prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s # How frequently to scrape targets
  evaluation_interval: 15s # How frequently to evaluate rules

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'node_exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9100'] # Assuming node_exporter runs on the same host

remote_write:
  - url: https://aps-workspaces.<YOUR_REGION>.amazonaws.com/workspaces/<YOUR_AMP_WORKSPACE_ID>/api/v1/remote_write
    sigv4:
      region: <YOUR_REGION>
      # You might need to specify a role ARN if cross-account
    queue_config:
      max_samples_per_send: 1000
      batch_send_deadline: 5s
      max_shards: 20
      min_shards: 1
Key fields
  • url: AMP remote_write endpoint — replace placeholders.
  • sigv4: lets Prometheus sign requests with AWS credentials.
  • queue_config: controls batching and concurrency for reliable sends.
Misconfiguration trap
Leaving <placeholders> unchanged or missing sigv4 region will prevent successful remote_write. Always validate Prometheus logs and Grafana Explore after deploying.

screens.title: Connecting AMP and AMG
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Managed Grafana acts as a managed Grafana workspace that can connect to AMP as a data source. When creating an AMG workspace, select Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus as a data source and link the AMP workspace. Authentication typically relies on IAM roles or the chosen identity provider; for demos the AWS IAM Identity Center is a straightforward option. A common operational error is incorrect IAM permissions: AMG must have the necessary IAM role or policy allowing it to query the AMP workspace. Another issue is misconfiguring the data source endpoint in Grafana or selecting the wrong workspace. After linking, always verify the connection in Grafana's Connections -> Data sources screen and use the Explore tab to run PromQL queries against AMP. Example checks include running a simple metric query such as node_cpu_seconds_total to ensure that metrics appear. The takeaway: connecting AMG to AMP is straightforward but pay careful attention to IAM and the exact AMP workspace endpoint to avoid connectivity problems. Connecting AMP and AMG means ensure amg has correct iam permissions and the amp workspace endpoint is selected as the grafana data source before building dashboards.. screens.title: PromQL Basics — selection and aggregation
screens.narratorSegment: PromQL is the language you use to operate on time-series in AMP. At its simplest, a metric name selects a set of time-series; adding label matchers narrows the selection. Functions like rate convert counter increases into per-second rates over a range vector such as five minutes. Aggregation operators like sum or avg group results by label dimensions using the by clause. A concrete example: rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]) computes the per-second average increase of the idle C P U counter over the last five minutes. Wrapping that in avg by (instance) or sum by (pod) aggregates across the chosen label. A common misconception is treating rate on gauges; rate is meant for counters, so use appropriate functions for gauges. Practice in Grafana's Explore tab to verify a query before using it in a dashboard. The key skill is composing selection, functions, and aggregations to answer operational questions like per-pod memory usage or cluster-wide C P U utilization. screens.title: CPU utilization example in PromQL
screens.narratorSegment: A common operational query computes C P U utilization by using the idle C P U counter and rate. The pattern subtracts idle percentage from 100 to get used C P U. For example, rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]) gives the per-second idle rate; averaging or summing by instance and multiplying by 100 converts to a percentage. The chapter provides a useful expression: 100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100). Use this in Grafana panels to show per-instance C P U utilization. A misconception is assuming the rate result is a percentage — it's a per-second rate of counter increase, so multiply by 100 and subtract from 100 to get utilization. Another practical note: ensure you select the right mode label and group by the correct label, for example instance or pod, depending on whether you scraped node exporters or container metrics. Validate in Explore and compare with host-level monitoring to ensure the query matches expected system metrics. CPU utilization example in PromQL means use rate on the idle cpu counter, aggregate by instance, convert to percent, and subtract from 100 to compute utilization.. In practical terms, calculate node or cluster cpu usage from idle counter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Use PromQL to convert counter rates into a percent utilization metric that is easy to visualize and alert on.
# Example PromQL to compute average CPU utilization per instance
100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100)
Misconception
Don't treat rate output as a percentage without converting; rate returns per-second increments and must be multiplied appropriately.

screens.title: Histogram percentiles with histogram_quantile
screens.narratorSegment: To compute percentiles from Prometheus histogram metrics, use histogram_quantile combined with rate and sum by bucket. Histogram metrics expose bucket counts with the _bucket suffix and a label le for the upper bound. The common pattern is histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))), which computes the 99th percentile of request durations over a five-minute range. This expression first calculates the per-second rate of each bucket, aggregates counts by bucket boundary, and then applies the histogram_quantile function to return the estimated percentile. A common error is forgetting the sum by (le) aggregation, which leads to incorrect inputs for histogram_quantile. Another pitfall is using a too-short range vector for sparse traffic; increase the window to capture sufficient samples. Validate the result by comparing p50, p90, and p99 across traffic spikes and use Grafana to visualize them as separate panels to spot tail latency behavior. The key skill is recognizing histogram bucket semantics and using the correct aggregation pattern for percentiles. Histogram percentiles with histogram_quantile means use histogram_quantile with sum by (le) and rate over an appropriate range vector to compute percentiles from histogram buckets.. In practical terms, compute p99 from bucketed request durations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Percentiles require the histogram bucket semantics. Use rate over buckets, aggregate by bucket boundary, then apply histogram_quantile to compute the desired percentile.
# Example PromQL for p99
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
Pitfalls
Missing sum by (le) or using an insufficient range window will yield inaccurate percentiles for low-traffic services.
Practical check
Visualize p50, p90, and p99 to understand tail latency and validate against synthetic load tests when possible.

screens.title: Terminal demo: set up AMP, Node Exporter, Prometheus, and AMG
screens.narratorSegment: This demo is a terminal-first walkthrough of the core steps to verify metrics flow end-to-end. The sequence starts by creating an AMP workspace, then launching an EC2 instance, installing Node Exporter and Prometheus on the same host, configuring Prometheus to scrape Node Exporter and remote_write to the AMP endpoint, and finally creating an AMG workspace and linking it to AMP. In the terminal you will run aws amp create-workspace with an alias, then install node_exporter and start it in the background. After that install Prometheus, create a prometheus. yml as shown in the chapter, and start Prometheus with that configuration. Verify the exporter with curl to port 9100 and check Prometheus targets for successful scrapes. In AMG, create a workspace, select AMP as a data source, and test a PromQL query like node_cpu_seconds_total to ensure data appears. A common mistake during this demo is not attaching an IAM role with AmazonPrometheusRemoteWriteAccess to the EC2 instance or mis-copying the AMP endpoint URL. The practical goal is to see metrics flow from exporter to AMP and display in AMG, and then challenge yourself to write a more advanced PromQL query for a dashboard panel.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Terminal Demo
Follow these terminal steps in sequence. Replace placeholders with your AMP workspace values and ensure the EC2 instance role includes AmazonPrometheusRemoteWriteAccess.
Create AMP workspace (CLI)
# Create an AMP workspace via AWS CLI
aws amp create-workspace --alias my-devops-workspace
Install Node Exporter (EC2)
wget https://github.com/prometheus/node_exporter/releases/download/v1.7.0/node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xvfz node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
cd node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64
./node_exporter & # Run in background
Install Prometheus
wget https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/releases/download/v2.49.1/prometheus-2.49.1.linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xvfz prometheus-2.49.1.linux-amd64.tar.gz
cd prometheus-2.49.1.linux-amd64
prometheus.yml (snippet)
# Replace YOUR_AMP_WORKSPACE_ENDPOINT with your AMP remote write URL
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'node_exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9100']

remote_write:
  - url: YOUR_AMP_WORKSPACE_ENDPOINT
    sigv4:
      region: <YOUR_REGION>
Validation steps
  • curl http://localhost:9100/metrics to confirm Node Exporter is up.
  • Open Prometheus targets to confirm successful scrapes.
  • In AMG Explore, run node_cpu_seconds_total to ensure AMP receives samples.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three core concepts to keep top of mind. First, AMP is a managed, Prometheus-compatible service that preserves your metric names and labels and absorbs storage and scaling responsibilities. Third, remote_write is the mechanism Prometheus uses to forward scraped samples to AMP for long-term storage. When you remember these three ideas—managed backend, exporter scraping model, and remote write—you can reason about architecture, troubleshoot why a metric isn't appearing, and choose the right tooling for Kubernetes and container workloads. Make sure you validate connectivity at each hop and keep IAM permissions and endpoints correct to avoid the most common failures. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore how Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana let teams keep the Prometheus model they trust while removing operational overhead. You will learn why organizations favor Prometheus-format metrics for containerized workloads, how exporters expose metrics, the role a local Prometheus server plays when forwarding data using remote write, and how Managed Grafana visualizes those metrics with PromQL queries. We'll use concrete examples: Node Exporter producing host metrics, a Prometheus server configured for remote write to an AMP workspace, and a Grafana panel that computes C P U utilization. I'll point out common pitfalls such as incorrect IAM permissions or misconfigured Grafana data sources, and a simple check to validate metrics flow. By the end you'll understand the end-to-end flow from exporter to query, what parts you manage, and what AMP and AMG manage for you, so you can plan a migration or deploy a new monitoring stack with confidence.

These learning objectives define practical competencies you will gain. First, you'll understand the benefits of Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus: why teams prefer a managed, Prometheus-compatible backend to avoid scaling and availability headaches. Second, you'll be able to configure exporters and Prometheus so your applications and nodes expose metrics correctly. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic to anchor the idea. You'll practice configuring remote write so a local Prometheus server forwards metrics to AMP instead of storing them locally. Finally, you'll learn to use Amazon Managed Grafana to build dashboards and author PromQL queries. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone you can use to self-check progress. Together these objectives move you from conceptual understanding to a hands-on ability to deploy, verify, and visualize Prometheus-format metrics in a managed AWS environment.

This page translates objectives into small, verifiable tasks you can complete. For AMP benefits you should be able to explain how retention, scaling, and multi-tenant managed storage differ from a self-hosted Prometheus cluster. For exporters, demonstrate installing Node Exporter and confirming its /metrics endpoint in a browser or with curl. For AMG, link an AMG workspace to AMP and open the Grafana Explore tab to validate queries. For PromQL, validate a simple query such as computing C P U utilization or using histogram_quantile for latency percentiles. Each task sharpens both configuration skill and operational judgement. We'll also cover the most common mistakes: exporters not reachable, Prometheus misconfigured to write to the wrong endpoint, or IAM roles not granting AMG the necessary permissions to query AMP. Completing these verified milestones means you can deploy and validate a basic AMP+AMG observability pipeline.

Start with the problem many teams face: self-hosted Prometheus is familiar and flexible but becomes difficult to operate at scale. You must manage storage, high availability, backups, and horizontal scaling when ingesting millions of samples. AMP addresses those operational concerns by offering a managed, Prometheus-compatible backend. That means you keep existing exporters, PromQL queries, and dashboards while shifting storage, scaling, and availability to the managed service. Contrast AMP with CloudWatch: CloudWatch is excellent for native AWS metrics and aggregated service telemetry, but it is not Prometheus-native. If your stack relies on Prometheus exporters or Kubernetes metrics, AMP preserves label semantics and PromQL semantics that CloudWatch may not. A common misconception is that AMP replaces all observability needs; instead, view AMP as a drop-in scalable backend for Prometheus data while CloudWatch remains useful for AWS-specific metrics. Example: when migrating a Kubernetes cluster, retaining Prometheus labels lets you reuse alerting rules and Grafana dashboards without rework. The takeaway is practical: choose AMP when you want Prometheus compatibility and to avoid running the storage layer yourself, and keep CloudWatch for service-level or platform events where it already excels.

Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed service that provides a Prometheus-compatible ingestion, storage, and query backend. In practice this means you can keep your existing exporters and PromQL queries but avoid running the distributed storage and scaling systems yourself. AMP accepts Prometheus remote write traffic, stores samples for months, and exposes an A P I that AMP-aware clients and Grafana can query. A concrete example: run a Prometheus server in your cluster that scrapes node_exporter and kube-state-metrics, and configure remote_write to forward those samples to your AMP workspace endpoint. AMP handles ingestion at scale, sharding, and retention so your operations team doesn't need to manage long-term storage. A common misconception is that AMP changes the Prometheus data model. It does not: AMP preserves metric names and labels, so existing alerts and dashboards continue to work. The practical takeaway is to treat AMP as a managed, drop-in backend that scales your Prometheus data and reduces operational toil. What is Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP)? means a managed, prometheus-compatible backend that ingests prometheus remote_write traffic and stores time-series metrics at scale.. In practical terms, a managed, prometheus-compatible time-series backend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Prometheus exporters are simple HTTP agents that expose application or host metrics in the Prometheus text format. The exporter model decouples metric collection from storage: exporters only expose metrics, and Prometheus scrapes them. Common exporters you will use include Node Exporter for host-level metrics like C P U, memory, and disk input and output; kube-state-metrics for Kubernetes object-level metrics such as pods and deployments; and application-specific exporters for software like Redis, MySQL, or Nginx. You can also instrument application code using Prometheus client libraries to expose custom application metrics. A concrete example: Node Exporter listens on port 9100 and exposes metrics at /metrics; Prometheus scrapes that endpoint at a configured interval. A frequent mistake is trying to push metrics directly from exporters to AMP; exporters are meant to be scraped by Prometheus. Instead, run a Prometheus server to scrape exporters and use Prometheus remote_write to forward metrics to AMP. Remember the practical rule: exporters expose, Prometheus scrapes, and AMP stores. This separation makes the pipeline modular and easier to debug. Prometheus Exporters — Role and common types means exporters expose metrics via http; prometheus scrapes them and then forwards samples to amp via remote_write.. In practical terms, how exporters expose metrics and which ones to use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the data flow is critical for reliable monitoring. The typical pipeline starts with exporters exposing metrics on HTTP endpoints. A Prometheus server scrapes these endpoints at a configured interval, converting the textual metrics into time-stamped samples. Instead of storing those samples locally, a Prometheus server can be configured with remote_write to forward samples to an AMP workspace endpoint. Remote_write batches samples and sends them to AMP with optional queue and shard settings to control throughput. AMP then performs ingestion, indexing, and long-term storage. For visualization, AMG connects to AMP as a data source and uses PromQL to query the stored time-series. A concrete scenario: you deploy Node Exporter on each node, configure a cluster-local Prometheus to scrape node exporters and kube-state-metrics, and enable remote_write to AMP. Common mistakes include forgetting to adjust scrape intervals, not tuning queue_config when high cardinality metrics produce a lot of samples, or using exporters that expose too-frequent metrics that overwhelm the queue. The practical check is to validate each step: curl the exporter, verify Prometheus target status, and confirm samples appear in Grafana Explore.

Let's walk through a concrete prometheus. yml snippet that configures scraping and remote_write to an AMP workspace. The configuration sets a global scrape_interval and evaluation_interval, defines scrape_configs for targets such as node_exporter, and includes a remote_write block pointing at the AMP workspace remote write URL. Important fields under remote_write include sigv4 for region authentication and queue_config which controls batching and throughput. A concrete example is shown in the visual code panel. Use this snippet as a template, replacing the placeholder workspace endpoint, region, and optionally a role ARN for cross-account setups.
